Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-1}^{1}-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{t}{|}_{-1}^{1}-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(e+{e}^{-1})-{e}^{t}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(e+{e}^{-1})-(e-{e}^{-1}) \\  & =2{e}^{-1}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,{e}^{-t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-t} & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t=-{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-1}^{1}-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t{e}^{-t}{|}_{-1}^{1}+{\int }_{-1}^{1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-{e}^{-1}-e)-{e}^{-t}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-{e}^{-1}-e)-({e}^{-1}-e) \\  & =-2{e}^{-1}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is false. We have ⟨f1(t),f2(t)⟩=⟨t,et⟩=∫−11tetdt Let's use integration by parts. We denote u=t⟹u′=1,v′=et⟹v=∫v′dt=∫etdt=et. Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain ∫−11tetdt=uv|−11−∫−11u′vdt=tet|−11−∫−11etdt=(e+e−1)−et|−11=(e+e−1)−(e−e−1)=2e−1≠0. This means that f1(t)⊥̸f2(t) with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement II is false. We have ⟨f1(t),f3(t)⟩=⟨t,e−t⟩=∫−11te−tdt Let's use integration by parts. We denote u=t⟹u′=1,v′=e−t⟹v=∫v′dt=∫e−tdt=−e−t. Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain ∫−11te−tdt=uv|−11−∫−11u′vdt=−te−t|−11+∫−11e−tdt=(−e−1−e)−e−t|−11=(−e−1−e)−(e−1−e)=−2e−1≠0. This means that f1(t)⊥̸f3(t) with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement III is false. Since f1(t)⊥̸f2(t), the set S is not orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."
